title: Cross-validation for longitudinal nuisance models optimizes prediction, not causal performance
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The general claim, that predictive cross-validation is the wrong criterion for a nuisance model whose purpose is causal, is correct and is not new. What the entry misses is that criteria other than prediction are already in use for the weight model specifically. Calibrated weights fitted with SuperLearner have been implemented and applied to longitudinal diabetes cohorts, and calibration is precisely a balance criterion rather than a prediction criterion. Super learner for weight estimation under unknown weight-model specification was studied for marginal structural models as early as 2017. So the entry’s claim that no selection criterion in routine use combines prediction with balance overstates: balance-based weight fitting exists and is published. The part that survives is the combination the entry actually asks for, a single loss spanning prediction, longitudinal balance, weight dispersion and an influence-function remainder, and the absence of a default library tuned that way. Cites 10.1109/jbhi.2022.3175862: Fits marginal structural model weights with SuperLearner under a calibration criterion rather than a prediction criterion, in a longitudinal EHR setting with dynamic regimes.. Cites 10.1002/sim.7266: Studies super learner for the weight model specifically, which is the nuisance component the entry says selection is blind for.. Cites 10.1002/sim.9568: Treats cross-validation for dynamic treatment regimes directly, in the presence of competing risks..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The estimator-selection question is coherent, but the methodological setup is incorrect. Identification follows from the observed-data law plus consistency, sequential exchangeability, positivity and a well-defined intervention; estimators do not themselves identify effects. The methods listed do not all require treatment, censoring and outcome nuisance models. An IP-weighted MSM generally models treatment and censoring mechanisms; the parametric g-formula models the conditional evolution of covariates and outcomes without requiring a treatment model; standard g-estimation combines a structural model with a treatment model; longitudinal TMLE uses sequential outcome regressions and treatment or censoring mechanisms. Prediction-optimal tuning need not minimize causal error, but near-zero probabilities can reflect the true treatment process and practical positivity rather than excessive adaptivity. Predictive cross-validation does not optimize balance or weight dispersion, although those quantities are functions of its predictions and can be assessed separately. An influence-function remainder is not generally observable because it depends on unknown nuisance errors. The assertion that no routine criterion exists is a literature-coverage claim outside this audit. The ltmle capability claim is unverified because calibration.json pins only TrialEmulation and no ltmle source is vendored under documentation/refs/packages/.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Inverted-prior search did not find a routine selection criterion that jointly optimizes treatment prediction, longitudinal balance, weight dispersion, and an influence-function remainder for longitudinal nuisance models. SuperLearner (as used by ltmle and related stacks) still cross-validates predictive risk; CV-TMLE and related work improve targeting of the final parameter after nuisance fitting but do not replace predictive CV for the treatment, censoring, and outcome libraries themselves. Collaborative TMLE (C-TMLE) is the closest prior art: it selects confounder models using a targeted, collaborative criterion rather than pure prediction, and longitudinal/scalable C-TMLE variants exist. That is covariate-and-collaborative selection for TMLE, not a multi-metric SuperLearner loss for sustained-regime MSM, g-formula, g-estimation, or LTMLE libraries. Point-treatment work on balance-versus-discrimination for propensity scores (for example Diaz on balancing criteria) does not cover sequential longitudinal nuisance selection. Package surfaces checked in search (ltmle SuperLearner interface, SuperLearner defaults, SAS SUPERLEARNER 2024/2025) still select on predictive CV. No 2024 to 2026 AJE/Epidemiology/SiM-style paper or CRAN default library was found that implements the combined causal objective the problem names. Searches included: causal cross-validation SuperLearner longitudinal TMLE balance weight dispersion; causal loss OR targeted cross-validation nuisance MSM; collaborative TMLE longitudinal SuperLearner; propensity SuperLearner balance loss 2023 to 2026.

GLM-5.2, third independent lens

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and well-scoped. It asserts that no selection criterion in routine use combines treatment prediction with longitudinal balance, weight dispersion, and an influence-function remainder—this is a claim about current practice, not about impossibility. The reason given for openness is structural: the causal loss (counterfactual contrast) is never observed, so there is no label to cross-validate against, and computable surrogates like balance are not proper decision-theoretic losses. This genuinely supports the problem being open. The one sentence about no default library being tuned for the causal objective touches on software, but the core claim is methodological. The severity is proportionate: a wrong default selection criterion would propagate bias into every downstream causal estimate.

Decision path

title: No mediated effect is defined for a sustained treatment strategy, and emulations report a proportion mediated anyway
text: EST-04 Partially addressed High priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: No mediated effect is defined for a sustained treatment strategy, and emulations report a proportion mediated anyway
text:
Statement
The target trial protocol has seven components: eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment, follow-up, outcome, causal contrast and analysis plan. None of them holds an intermediate variable, so a mediator enters an emulation only as an analysis appended after the total effect is estimated. The methods borrowed for that appendix are stated for a randomly assigned point or fixed longitudinal exposure with the mediator assessed at planned visits: the mediational g-formula for time-varying exposures and mediators, interventional effects for multiple mediators, path-specific effects for repeatedly measured mediators under time-varying confounding, and a 2026 extension of the last to competing risks. None is stated for a sustained strategy realized by cloning, artificial censoring and inverse-probability-of-censoring weights, nor for a sequential emulation in which one person contributes to many trials, and in both of those designs the population followed under each strategy is constructed by the analysis rather than given. Applied emulations report mechanism regardless, as a proportion mediated on a hazard or subdistribution-hazard scale: 2.4 percent and 6.5 percent of the semaglutide effect on adult-onset seizure through hemoglobin A1c, 8.7 percent of the cardiovascular benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors through regression of steatotic liver disease. A proportion mediated on a hazard scale is not a ratio of counterfactual risk contrasts and matches none of the estimands the identification results cover. Three objects are missing and each is nameable: a mediated estimand defined for a sustained strategy, an identification result for it when censoring is artificial, and a protocol component that requires the mediator, its measurement times and its intercurrent-event strategy to be fixed before the analysis.

title: No mediated effect is defined for a sustained treatment strategy, and emulations report a proportion mediated anyway
text:
Why it is open
Two requirements conflict and no estimand satisfies both. Natural direct and indirect effects carry the mechanistic reading and need a cross-world independence that no experiment can check, and that fails outright once a confounder of the mediator and the outcome is affected by treatment, which is the ordinary situation across follow-up. Interventional effects drop the cross-world condition and are identified from a single world, and they fail the sharp mediational null: an interventional indirect effect can be nonzero when no individual has any mediated effect at all, so a nonzero estimate does not license the sentence about mechanism it is written to support. Emulation adds an obstacle the trial setting does not have, because under cloning and artificial censoring the variable that mediates is frequently the same variable that triggers deviation from the strategy, so it enters the censoring weight and the mediation formula at once and the weighting already conditions on part of the mediator path. The mediator is also recorded when a patient attends care rather than on a schedule, so the repeated mediator history that every longitudinal identification result assumes is itself selectively observed. Nobody has worked the join out because the applied demand is met far more cheaply: point-treatment mediation software runs on the weighted cohort and returns a percentage.

title: No mediated effect is defined for a sustained treatment strategy, and emulations report a proportion mediated anyway
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Vansteelandt S, Linder M, Vandenberghe S, Steen J, Madsen J. Mediation analysis of time-to-event endpoints accounting for repeatedly measured mediators subject to time-varying confounding. Stat Med 2019;38(24):4828-4840
Identifies a path-specific effect through a repeatedly measured mediator under time-varying confounding, for a randomly assigned treatment with the mediator measured at planned visits, and states that the effect along all pathways intercepting one or more mediators is not identified without overly stringent assumptions.


Tai AS, Lin SH, Chu YC, Yu T, Puhan MA, VanderWeele TJ. Causal mediation analysis with multiple time-varying mediators. Epidemiology 2023;34(1):8-19
Extends the mediational g-formula from a single mediator to several time-varying mediators, with nonparametric identification for two variants and an R implementation, which is the supply the candidate assumed was absent.


Vansteelandt S, Daniel RM. Interventional effects for mediation analysis with multiple mediators. Epidemiology 2017;28(2):258-265
Defines interventional direct and indirect effects for multiple mediators, identified without a cross-world condition, which are the estimands an emulation would have to adopt if it wanted identification from a single world.


Miles CH. On the causal interpretation of randomised interventional indirect effects. J R Stat Soc Series B Stat Methodol 2023;85(4):1154-1172
Shows that randomized interventional indirect effects do not satisfy the sharp null criterion without stronger assumptions, so a nonzero estimate is compatible with no individual-level mediation; this is the half of the conflict that the applied switch to interventional effects does not resolve.


Moreno-Betancur M, Moran P, Becker D, Patton GC, Carlin JB. Mediation effects that emulate a target randomised trial: Simulation-based evaluation of ill-defined interventions on multiple mediators. Stat Methods Med Res 2021;30(6):1395-1412
Defines interventional effects explicitly as contrasts in a target trial of hypothetical interventions on several mediators, estimated by g-computation; the closest existing template, and the trial it specifies is a trial of mediator interventions rather than an emulation of a sustained treatment strategy.


Domingo-Relloso A, Zhang Y, Wang Z, et al. A path-specific effect approach to mediation analysis with time-varying mediators and time-to-event outcomes accounting for competing risks. Stat Med 2026;45:e70425
Adds competing events to path-specific mediation with repeatedly measured mediators by treating the competing event as a nested mediator, with a mediational g-formula algorithm and simulation evidence.


Leigh L, Hinwood M, Oldmeadow C, et al. Which factors mediate the effect of childhood socioeconomic disadvantage on mental health in young adulthood? A protocol for a target trial emulation using linked administrative data from New South Wales, Australia. BMJ Open 2026;16(3):e109541
An emulation protocol that prespecifies an interventional mediation analysis across several mediators, which is what practice looks like when the mediator is fixed in the protocol rather than added afterward.


Eun Y, Bong S, Koh HY, et al. Semaglutide and risk of adult-onset seizure: a target trial emulation. Neurology 2026;107(1):e218174
Applies a longitudinal path-specific framework derived for a randomized trial to a weighted emulation in electronic health records and reports mediation through hemoglobin A1c as 2.4 percent and 6.5 percent.


Jang H, Kim Y, Lim YK, et al. Outcomes of oral antidiabetic drugs in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: a nationwide target trial emulation study. Clin Mol Hepatol 2026;32(2):737-750
Reports that regression of steatotic liver disease accounts for 8.7 percent of the cardiovascular benefit, on a subdistribution-hazard scale, without naming the mediated estimand or its identification conditions.

title: No mediated effect is defined for a sustained treatment strategy, and emulations report a proportion mediated anyway
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Make the mediator a protocol component: name the intermediate variable, the times at which it is to be assessed, and the strategy for every intercurrent event that can precede it, so the mechanism question is fixed alongside eligibility and treatment strategies instead of being chosen once the total effect is known. Derive interventional direct and indirect effects for a sustained strategy under cloning and artificial censoring, and state what the estimand becomes when the mediator history enters the censoring weight; the tractable first step is a worked identification result for one time-varying mediator under a static strategy with a grace period, which is the design most emulations already run. Report the two mediator regimes as counterfactual risks at a stated horizon, on the same scale as the total effect the emulation already reports, rather than as a proportion mediated on a hazard scale. State for whichever effect is used whether it satisfies the sharp mediational null, so a reader can tell whether a nonzero estimate is evidence about mechanism or evidence about a distributional shift.

title: No mediated effect is defined for a sustained treatment strategy, and emulations report a proportion mediated anyway
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Searched the 1,376-record screened corpus rather than answering from memory. The emulation-specific half of the entry survives. […]
4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Searched the 1,376-record screened corpus rather than answering from memory. The emulation-specific half of the entry survives. Mediation terms ANDed with cloning, artificial censoring or censoring weights return four records, and none of them is a method: two are applied emulations that use clone-censor-weight and mention mediation in passing, one is a drug-wide screen, one is a 2013 collider-stratification example. Mediation ANDed with sustained or dynamic strategies or grace periods returns two records, both applied. The phrase proportion mediated returns zero records in the whole screened corpus, so the applied instances the entry cites sit outside the methodological literature entirely, which is consistent with the entry’s point that the reporting practice has outrun the estimand. Nothing in the corpus proposes an intermediate variable as a protocol component. The caveat is that the entry frames the estimand problem as a conflict between two families, natural effects needing a cross-world condition and interventional effects failing the sharp mediational null, and a third family exists in the corpus and was constructed for exactly that dilemma. Separable effects decompose the treatment rather than intervene on the mediator, and were defined for a longitudinal mediator with a survival outcome in 2018, generalized to time-varying structures with weaker identification conditions in 2021, and given g-formula identification conditions for longitudinal mediation in 2024. A reader given the entry as written would not learn that the escape route exists. The general-methods half of the entry is also weaker than the corpus supports: the mediational g-formula for time-varying exposures, mediators and confounders sits in the corpus from 2016 and 2017 with a parametric algorithm and released software, which the entry acknowledges in its rationale but its statement does not.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. The valid core is narrower than the statement. Reporting a proportion mediated from hazard or subdistribution-hazard ratios does not generally yield a fraction of a counterfactual risk effect, and applying point-treatment mediation software after clone-censor weighting does not generally identify a longitudinal mediated effect. The sharp-null criticism of randomized interventional indirect effects is also valid. However, fixed longitudinal exposure histories are static sustained strategies, and existing mediational g-formula work already defines direct and indirect effects and gives longitudinal identification results under sequential exchangeability and positivity. Cloning and artificial censoring are estimation devices, not new interventions or populations. Conditioning an artificial-censoring model on mediator history measured before censoring can correct selection; it does not itself condition the causal contrast on that mediator. When the mediator also determines a dynamic treatment rule, the intervention ordering and path-specific estimand require explicit definition, but this is not proof that no mediated estimand exists. Repeated participation in sequential trials primarily changes the target distribution, dependence structure, and variance calculation, not whether mediation counterfactuals can be defined. Likewise, an eighth universal protocol component is unnecessary because mediator interventions, measurement times, causal contrasts, intercurrent-event handling, and analysis can be prespecified within the existing strategy and analysis-plan components. The assertion that treatment-induced mediator-outcome confounding makes cross-world independence fail outright is too strong: it generally defeats standard nonparametric identification rather than logically forcing every possible cross-world restriction to be false. A genuine gap remains for defensible implementation when grace-period or dynamic strategies interact with the mediator, mediator visits are informative, and clone-censor and mediator-process weights must be combined. That is a specialized extension and reporting problem, not a missing foundation for all sustained strategies. It is critical only when mechanism is a decision-grade objective; it does not invalidate an otherwise valid total-effect emulation. No named package capability is asserted here, so no package claim was adjudicated. Cites doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001555: Defines direct and indirect effects for longitudinal exposure histories and supplies nonparametric identification results. Static sustained regimes are included in that class, although clone-specific estimation and informative observation remain unresolved.. Cites doi:10.1177/0962280221998409: Shows that mediator interventions and mediation contrasts can be specified explicitly as a target trial and estimated by g-computation, contradicting the claim that the standard seven-component template forces mediation to be appended post hoc..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Inverted-prior search for a mediated estimand, identification result, or software path under sustained strategies realized by cloning, artificial censoring and IPCW, or under sequential trial emulation, did not turn up a resolving paper or package. Highest-yield check was the report’s own prior_work: Vansteelandt et al. 2019 (path-specific, randomly assigned treatment, planned mediator visits), Tai et al. 2023 (mediational g-formula with multiple time-varying mediators and R code), Vansteelandt and Daniel 2017 (interventional effects), Miles 2023 (interventional effects fail the sharp mediational null), Moreno-Betancur et al. 2021 (target trial of mediator interventions, not a treatment-strategy emulation under cloning), Domingo-Relloso et al. 2026 (path-specific plus competing risks for repeatedly measured mediators), Leigh et al. 2026 (protocol that prespecifies interventional mediation), and the applied TTE reports Eun et al. 2026 and Jang et al. 2026 (proportion mediated on hazard or subdistribution-hazard scales). Those works formalize or apply mediation for point, fixed longitudinal, or naturally time-varying exposure processes with planned or modeled mediator visits; none states an estimand or identification formula for a strategy population constructed by cloning and artificial censoring, nor for one person contributing to many sequential emulations. Broader 2024–2026 searches across AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/Stat Med/Biometrics-type venues, arXiv stat.ME, and medRxiv for combinations of mediation or path-specific or interventional indirect effects with cloning, clone-censor-weight, artificial censoring, sustained strategy, sequential trial emulation, or grace period returned applied TTEs that append mediation after a total effect, methods primers that list mediation and CCW as separate topics, and classic time-varying mediation (Lin et al. 2017 mediational g-formula for time-varying exposures; Zheng and van der Laan-type longitudinal mediation) that still assume an observed exposure process rather than an analysis-constructed strategy cohort. Package surface checks for TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, and related tools did not surface a merged feature for mediated contrasts under CCW or sequential emulation. TARGET 2025 (Cashin et al., JAMA) still organizes reporting around the standard target-trial protocol components and does not add a required mediator, measurement-time, and intercurrent-event block. The closest adjacent proposal is Gonzalez-Perez, Wanis, Sarvet, and Stensrud (arXiv:2508.10702, 2025), which encodes separable effects for sustained treatments with identifying functionals and doubly robust estimators; that is a path-type decomposition of treatment components under sustained use, not classical mediation through a measured intermediate (for example HbA1c) when that intermediate also drives artificial censoring weights. Separable-effects theory therefore does not close the three nameable gaps in the statement: a mediated estimand for a sustained strategy under cloning or sequential emulation, identification when the mediator history enters the censoring weight, and a protocol component that fixes the mediator before analysis. Miles 2023 further keeps the natural-versus-interventional interpretability conflict open rather than solved. Queries run included: mediation + cloning/artificial censoring/CCW; interventional mediation + sustained strategy/IPCW; path-specific + grace period/clone-censor; sequential trial emulation + mediation; target trial + proportion mediated; arXiv/medRxiv sustained treatment + mediation/indirect/path-specific 2024–2026; TARGET guideline + mediator; CRAN/GitHub mediation hooks for the listed TTE and g-methods packages. Finding nothing that joins the pieces is itself the finding: the problem remains open as stated.

GLM-5.2, third independent lens

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and well-scoped. It identifies a genuine structural gap: existing mediation estimands (natural effects, interventional effects, path-specific effects) are developed for randomized exposures with scheduled mediator visits, not for sustained strategies implemented via cloning, artificial censoring, and IPCW. The reason given for openness is structural, not merely about current practice: (1) natural effects require cross-world independence that fails when treatment affects mediator-outcome confounders; (2) interventional effects sacrifice the sharp mediational null, so nonzero estimates do not license mechanistic claims; (3) emulation introduces a join problem where the mediator may simultaneously trigger censoring and enter the mediation formula, and the mediator history is selectively observed at care visits rather than on schedule. These are real difficulties, not inconveniences. The claim correctly avoids impossibility language—it says ‘nobody has worked the join out,’ framing this as an absence of work rather than a structural barrier. The critique that proportion-mediated on a hazard scale is not a ratio of counterfactual risk contrasts is mathematically correct and proportionate. The cited works (Vansteelandt 2019, Tai 2023, Vansteelandt & Daniel 2017, Miles 2023, Moreno-Betancur 2021, Domingo-Relloso 2026) genuinely do not address sustained strategies under cloning/censoring; Moreno-Betancur 2021 is the closest but specifies a trial of mediator interventions, not a sustained treatment strategy. The Leigh 2026 protocol prespecifies mediation but does not derive the identification result. The applied papers (Eun 2026, Jang 2026) report percentages without naming estimands, which is consistent with the claim. The severity (High) is proportionate: these percentages appear in clinical journals and may be read as mechanistic evidence. One limitation: the absence claim (‘nobody has worked the join out’) is inherently difficult to verify without search, but the structural arguments for why it remains open are sound and the cited literature does not fill the gap.

Decision path

title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
text: EST-02 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
text:
Statement
An internally valid estimate need not apply to the health system, population or calendar period where the decision will be made. Weighting, outcome modeling and doubly robust transport estimators all exist, and all of them require that the effect modifiers be measured, that the populations overlap, and that effects be conditionally exchangeable across samples. Applied transport work still mostly uses conventional sampling weights or outcome models despite the more flexible alternatives. The deeper issue is that transporting an observational estimate stacks the sampling-exchangeability assumption on top of the treatment-exchangeability assumption, and no current reporting practice shows how the two compound or which one a given discrepancy should be charged to.

title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
text:
Why it is open
Both assumption sets are untestable and they fail in correlated ways: a health system whose case mix differs is usually also one whose confounding structure and treatment availability differ, so a single sensitivity parameter cannot represent the joint failure. Unmeasured effect modification is not detectable in the source population, since by construction it is a variable nobody measured. Combining transport with flexible representation learning risks erasing the very effect modification that transport is supposed to preserve, because predictive invariance and causal invariance are different properties.

title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Westreich D, Edwards JK, Lesko CR, Stuart E, Cole SR. Transportability of trial results using inverse odds of sampling weights. Am J Epidemiol 2017;186(8):1010-1014
Gives the inverse-odds-of-sampling weighting estimator for transporting a trial result to a target population.


Manke-Reimers M, et al. When, why and how are estimated effects transported between populations? A scoping review. Eur J Epidemiol 2025
Maps what applied transport studies actually do, which is where the finding that flexible estimators are underused comes from.

title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop causal representation learning for transportability that balances sites only on representations sufficient for effect modification, rather than on everything predictive, and combine it with targeted standardization and site-level random effects. Derive bounds under unmeasured effect modification and report them alongside the point estimate, so a transported number carries its own fragility. Simulate sites that differ in covariates, treatment mechanisms, baseline hazards and effect modifiers separately, so that the contribution of each source of non-transportability is measurable rather than confounded with the others.

title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Transport methods are reaching emulation practice faster than the entry allows. A 2026 Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics paper performs post hoc population standardization of trial emulation studies in claims data within RCT-DUPLICATE, which is transport applied to the benchmarking corpus itself. Nurse home visiting was emulated in the policy-relevant population using targeted learning and transport, and the scoping review the entry cites documents the practice broadly. What survives is the compounding claim: no reporting practice shows how sampling exchangeability and treatment exchangeability compound, or which of the two a discrepancy should be charged to. Cites 10.1002/cpt.70241: Standardizes emulations to trial populations inside the largest benchmarking program, which is transport applied where the entry says it is underused.. Cites 10.1093/ije/dyac092: Combines the target trial framework with transport and targeted learning to reach a policy-relevant population..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. Transporting an observational effect does require distinct treatment-exchangeability and cross-sample exchangeability conditions, together with treatment and sampling positivity. The report overstates what must be measured: identification needs a sufficient transport set, not literally every effect modifier. Effect modifiers that do not differ across samples or are irrelevant after conditioning need not all be observed. A scalar sensitivity parameter can represent an aggregate joint bias, although it cannot uniquely decompose that bias without additional restrictions. The inability to charge a discrepancy to one assumption is chiefly nonidentification, not merely absent reporting. Representation learning or site random effects do not restore identification by themselves. The empirical claim about current practice is outside this technical vote.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Transport estimators (IOSW, outcome modeling, doubly robust/TMLE, calibration) are mature for trials and increasingly documented for observational sources; that is already acknowledged by the report’s Westreich citation and does not close the problem. The open core is accounting: transporting an observational estimate stacks treatment-exchangeability on sampling-exchangeability, both largely untestable, and no standard reporting practice decomposes a discrepancy between those failure modes. Scelo et al. (Front Epidemiol 2024; 10.3389/fepid.2024.1335241) explicitly lists the internal-validity and external-validity assumption blocks side by side, notes that most are untestable, and demonstrates TMLE transport from an observational birth cohort to a registry target; that formalizes the stack and does not provide joint sensitivity or attribution. Manke-Reimers et al. (Eur J Epidemiol 2025; 10.1007/s10654-025-01217-w), already cited, maps applied transport studies and underuse of flexible estimators; a scoping review of practice is evidence the gap remains, not a solution. Adamson et al. (Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf 2026; 10.1002/pds.70396) offers a stepwise transportability framework for comparative effectiveness and urges sensitivity for unmeasured effect modifiers, e-values, and tipping-point analyses; that is guidance and one-parameter sensitivity, not a joint compounding account that charges residual bias to confounding versus selection/effect-modification structure. Separate sensitivity tools for unmeasured confounding and for unmeasured selection/effect modification exist; they do not identify effects when both fail in correlated ways, and the discipline rule forbids treating sensitivity as solving identification. Causal representation learning for transport that preserves effect modification (rather than predictive invariance) remains workshop/early-methods work; no 2024–2026 applied TTE package (lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, TrialEmulation, zEpid) was found that ships joint internal-plus-external fragility bounds with attribution. Queries run: transportability observational compounding/joint sensitivity; unmeasured effect modification bounds transport; Manke-Reimers and Adamson follow-ups; Scelo 2024 full text; CRL transport effect modifiers; CRAN/GitHub keyword checks for transport modules. Vote open: methods and guidance expanded; the compounding-accounting and attribution problem as stated is not solved.

GLM-5.2, third independent lens

open / supported. The claim is coherent and pitched at the right level of generality. It accurately describes the compounding of sampling-exchangeability and treatment-exchangeability assumptions in transportability, and notes the lack of reporting practices to disentangle them. The reasons given for it being open (correlated failures of untestable assumptions, undetectable unmeasured effect modification, and the tension between predictive and causal invariance in representation learning) are valid and support the claim being open.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1/4) → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex

title: No procedure bounds the bias a comparator sampling scheme introduces before the study is run
text: ELG-03 Overstated Medium-high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: No procedure bounds the bias a comparator sampling scheme introduces before the study is run
text:
Statement
An emulation without an active comparator often builds its reference arm by drawing matched comparators from a population registry. Three schemes are in use: sampling with replacement, sampling without replacement in random order, and sampling without replacement in chronological order. They are not interchangeable. Sampling without replacement in random order conditions on the future, because a comparator consumed by a later-diagnosed patient was necessarily alive at that later date and is thereby removed from the pool available to an earlier one; this is the immortal time mechanism operating on the comparator arm rather than on the treated. Sampling without replacement in chronological order fails instead by exhaustion, leaving almost a fifth of a 347,882 patient heart failure cohort unmatched at five comparators per patient and returning a reference arm skewed young once unmatched patients are dropped. Which failure dominates, and in which direction, depends on the sampling ratio and on the comparators’ own outcome risk: at one comparator per patient the three schemes nearly coincide, and at five per patient in an elderly cohort they do not. No procedure bounds the resulting bias from quantities available before the analysis, so the scheme is picked by convention and its consequences are read off afterward, one dataset at a time.

title: No procedure bounds the bias a comparator sampling scheme introduces before the study is run
text:
Why it is open
The bias is a property of the joint distribution of index dates, comparator survival and pool depletion, so it cannot be recovered from the sampled cohort alone: the counterfactual is the comparison cohort that a different scheme would have produced, and only one scheme is ever run. The magnitude is setting-specific rather than universal, and the one empirical demonstration that exists is confined to a single national registry, one disease and two outcomes, with its own report stating that it does not quantify the differences in general. The literature cannot supply the missing calibration either, because most published studies using this design do not report which scheme they used. Nor is it a matter of adjustment after the fact: the scheme is executed during cohort construction, before any model is fitted, so no estimator downstream can price a choice that has already determined who is in the comparison arm.

title: No procedure bounds the bias a comparator sampling scheme introduces before the study is run
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Heide-Jorgensen U, et al. Sampling strategies for selecting general population comparison cohorts. Clin Epidemiol 2018;10:1325-1337
Compares the three schemes against index cohorts whose true outcome rates are known by construction, shows sampling without replacement in random order inflates comparator outcome rates when comparators are at substantial risk, and states that it does not provide a way to quantify the differences in general.


Suissa S. Immortal time bias in pharmacoepidemiology. Am J Epidemiol 2008;167(4):492-499
Characterizes the conditioning-on-the-future mechanism for the treated arm, which is the same mechanism that acts here on comparator availability, without treating comparator sampling as a site where it can arise.


Hernan MA, Robins JM. Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 2016;183(8):758-764
Requires the comparator to be specified as a trial would specify it, which makes the question askable but does not reach the sampling procedure that realizes it.


Arnold K, Antunes L, Coles B, et al. Application of the target trial emulation framework to external comparator studies. Front Drug Saf Regul 2024
Applies the protocol components to externally constructed comparison arms, where the same construction step sits, and addresses eligibility and time zero rather than the order in which eligible comparators are consumed.


Cashin AG, Hansford HJ, Hernan MA, et al. Transparent reporting of observational studies emulating a target trial: the TARGET statement. JAMA 2025
Requires the comparator and its emulation to be reported; it does not require the sampling scheme that produced the comparison cohort, which is the item whose absence makes the published literature uninformative here.

title: No procedure bounds the bias a comparator sampling scheme introduces before the study is run
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Derive the bias in the comparator hazard as a function of the three quantities an analyst knows before sampling: the sampling ratio, the size of the eligible pool relative to the index cohort within matching strata, and the comparator baseline hazard. The random-order case is tractable analytically, since depletion of the pool by later index dates is a known selection on survival, and it should yield a bound rather than a point correction. Simulate across sampling ratios and comparator risk to locate where the schemes separate, using the design in which index-cohort rates are known by construction so that error is measurable rather than inferred. Make the scheme, the ratio, and the count of unmatched index patients reportable items, since a scheme that leaves a fifth of patients unmatched has changed the study population and not only the reference arm. Sampling with replacement avoids both failures at the cost of dependence between observations, so quantify what that dependence costs in variance and settle whether it is the default.

title: No procedure bounds the bias a comparator sampling scheme introduces before the study is run
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. In matched external-comparator designs with high sampling fractions, random-order sampling without replacement can select on future survival or event-free status, while chronological sampling without replacement can deplete sparse matching strata. If only the realized matched cohort is retained and no adequate sampling-frame information or identifying assumptions are available, the comparator risk under an alternative scheme is not point identified. No nontrivial universal bound follows from the sampling ratio, aggregate pool ratio, and marginal baseline hazard alone. Analysts should retain the source frame, prespecify and report the scheme and unmatched counts, rerun feasible schemes, and use design-based adjustment or sensitivity analysis when its assumptions are supportable.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported-with-caveat): Searched against the 1,376-record screened corpus rather than from memory. Exactly one record addresses the object of this entry: the same 2018 Clinical Epidemiology study the entry cites. […]
4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Searched against the 1,376-record screened corpus rather than from memory. Exactly one record addresses the object of this entry: the same 2018 Clinical Epidemiology study the entry cites. The searches that would surface a competing treatment return nothing: zero records for risk set sampling, zero for population comparator, zero for comparator selection, and the only record matching sampling with replacement is that same paper. The adjacent literature is the external control and external comparator work, twelve records, and it is about adjusting a comparison arm to a trial population by weighting or matching, not about the order in which eligible comparators are consumed from a finite pool; the three of those records held in full text contain no occurrence of with replacement, without replacement, chronological order or risk set. The mechanism itself is not novel, since conditioning on the future is Suissa’s immortal time bias, but no work applies it to comparator pool depletion or bounds the result. The caveat is on scope rather than on existence. The cited study’s own headline is that the three schemes agree in the general population setting and separate only when comparators carry substantial outcome risk, and that the separation largely disappears at one comparator per patient; the entry states this, and a reader should not take the failure as general to matched comparator designs.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The future-conditioning mechanism under random-order sampling without replacement is correct, and chronological sampling can exhaust sparse matching strata at high sampling ratios. The statement nevertheless overreaches. Bias is undefined until a target comparator distribution, outcome scale, and effect estimand are specified; differences between sampled cohorts are not automatically causal-effect bias. Exhaustion is not unique to chronological sampling, and sampling with replacement guarantees matches only in strata containing at least one eligible comparator. The alternative cohorts are also not intrinsically counterfactual or unavailable: when the source registry and sampling frame are retained, all schemes can be rerun before effect estimation. Known inclusion probabilities, standardization, or selection weighting can address some sampling effects when the necessary frame variables, outcome information, positivity, and identifying assumptions hold. Nonparametric recovery generally fails only when the analyst retains the realized cohort without adequate frame information or when relevant target strata have zero inclusion probability. Conversely, no nontrivial universal bound can be obtained from the sampling ratio, aggregate pool ratio, and marginal baseline hazard alone. Joint information about index dates, matching strata, eligibility histories, survival, competing events, and outcome risk is required; distributions sharing the proposed three summaries can produce different directions and magnitudes. A useful calibration method under explicit assumptions remains an open roadmap item, but the asserted universal absence of procedures and downstream remedies is false, and the severity is substantial only for high sampling fractions in sparse, high-risk strata.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Under an inverted prior, the literature still treats pre-analysis bias bounds for general-population comparator sampling as missing. Heide-Jørgensen et al. (Clin Epidemiol 2018;10:1325-1337; doi:10.2147/CLEP.S164456) remains the central evidence: it demonstrates that sampling without replacement in random order can inflate comparator outcome rates via conditioning on the future, that chronological sampling without replacement fails by exhaustion (nearly one-fifth unmatched at 5:1 in a 347,882 heart-failure cohort, with a younger residual reference arm), and that the three schemes nearly coincide at 1:1 but separate at 5:1 when comparators are at high risk. Its own Discussion states the decisive limitation: the study “did not present means of quantifying the size of these differences in general.” That is documentation of the phenomenon, not a bound recoverable from sampling ratio, pool-to-index size within matching strata, and comparator baseline hazard before sampling is run.


Searches for a later resolving method returned none. Queries covered: (1) the paper’s own limitation language and its citations; (2) “sampling with/without replacement” + “general population comparison cohort” + chronological/random order + bias/bound/quantify, restricted to 2019–2026; (3) AJE, Epidemiology, IJE, EJE, JCE, PDS, Clin Epidemiol, Stat Med, SMMR, Biometrics, Biostatistics, BMC Med Res Methodol, Observational Studies, BMJ/JAMA/AIM, plus arXiv stat.ME/AP and medRxiv; (4) MatchIt, WeightIt, TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, cobalt, and related packages for a pre-analysis bias bound for registry comparator sampling (they implement with/without replacement for propensity matching, a different design); (5) TARGET 2025, Arnold et al. Front Drug Saf Regul 2024, STaRT-RWE/HARPER, ENCePP, FDA/EMA external-control guidance. What appears after 2018 is mostly applied uptake: Danish and other registry studies cite Heide-Jørgensen and default to sampling with replacement (or 1:1). That is a design convention, not a bound. Iwagami (Ann Clin Epidemiol 2022) discusses with/without-replacement tradeoffs for matching but supplies no pre-run bias formula for the three schemes. Austin-style PSM order and with/without-replacement results address treated–untreated matching within a study population, not index-date assignment of general-population comparators under pool depletion. TARGET requires reporting the comparator and its emulation, not the sampling scheme that produced the comparison arm, so the published literature remains largely uninformative for calibration.
A method paper that only proposes or recommends with replacement without evaluating a general bound would still leave the problem open. A sensitivity analysis after sampling would price consequences of a choice already executed, not bound bias from quantities known before cohort construction. No retrieved work derives the comparator-hazard bias as a function of the three pre-sampling quantities named in the agenda, or provides a validated simulation protocol that yields bounds rather than one-dataset case reports. Status therefore remains open; the statement is proportionate to the evidence.

GLM-5.2, third independent lens

abstain / overstated. The claim asserts that ‘No procedure bounds the resulting bias from quantities available before the analysis,’ which reads as a structural impossibility. However, the report’s own proposed direction (‘Derive the bias in the comparator hazard as a function of the three quantities an analyst knows before sampling… it should yield a bound’) demonstrates that the problem is not structurally impossible but rather a gap in current methodology. The claim is overstated, wearing the language of impossibility for what is actually an absence of a standard procedure. I abstain on the status axis because I cannot verify whether such a procedure has already been derived in the literature.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Statement
Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information therefore selects on laboratory testing, clinical documentation and specialist access, which differ systematically from the excluded patients. Weighting methods for missing eligibility have recently been developed and the literature remains small. The harder version of the problem is that eligibility is latent rather than merely missing: an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested, and the missingness itself may depend on treatment anticipation or on the impending outcome.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Why it is open
Missing-at-random conditional on the recorded history is not credible here, because the recording decision is a clinical judgment informed by exactly the severity that predicts the outcome. Distinguishing latent eligibility from missing measurement requires a validation source in which the criterion was assessed for everyone, and such sources are rare and rarely representative. Imputing the value and imputing eligibility are different operations with different targets, and the literature has not separated them.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Benz L, et al. Adjusting for selection bias due to missing eligibility criteria in emulated target trials. Am J Epidemiol 2025
Develops weighting for missing eligibility information in emulated trials, the first direct treatment of the problem.


Wang, et al. An operational target trial emulation framework for causal inference using electronic health records. npj Digit Med 2026
Sets out how each protocol component, eligibility included, is realized against record-level data and where the realization is partial.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Model true eligibility and its observation jointly, using validation records where a criterion was assessed for everyone to anchor the measurement model. Compare multiple imputation, inverse-probability-of-eligibility weighting, doubly robust selection correction and partial-identification bounds on the same data, since they make different assumptions and currently no one knows which are tolerable. Report the eligible population under each approach alongside the effect estimate, because a method that changes who is in the trial has changed the estimand and should be read that way.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The entry says the literature on missing eligibility is small. It is small and it is larger than the one paper the entry cites. […]
4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The entry says the literature on missing eligibility is small. It is small and it is larger than the one paper the entry cites. A 2026 Statistics in Medicine paper treats missingness in eligibility criteria for target trial emulation in electronic health records with survival outcomes, alongside the 2025 American Journal of Epidemiology weighting paper the entry already carries. The harder claim, that eligibility is latent rather than missing and that an absent value is consistent with both a failed criterion and an untested patient, is not addressed by either and stands. Cites 10.1002/sim.70500: A second and more recent direct treatment of the problem, which the entry’s claim of a very small literature should acknowledge.. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwae471: The weighting approach the entry already cites..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. Restricting analysis to records with observed eligibility can cause selection bias, but systematic differences between included and excluded patients do not alone establish bias for a specified causal estimand. Identification depends on conditional exchangeability for the observation or selection process and adequate observed support. When true eligibility is missing not at random, the effect among truly eligible patients is generally not identified from the main data alone. However, assessing the criterion for everyone in a validation source is sufficient, not necessary. A probability validation subsample, auxiliary-variable restrictions, explicit parametric assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or partial-identification methods can also inform the problem. If eligibility is a deterministic threshold of an underlying measurement, imputing that measurement and deriving eligibility can target the same population as directly imputing eligibility. Changing imputed membership across draws represents missing-data uncertainty and does not automatically change the estimand. Existing weighting work addresses an important identified-assumption case, while the unrestricted latent-eligibility problem remains open. Cites doi:10.1093/aje/kwae471: Provides a weighting approach for selection arising from missing eligibility information under identifying assumptions; it does not nonparametrically identify unrestricted missing-not-at-random latent eligibility..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Inverted prior: treat missing-eligibility selection as already handled, then check what exists. Three direct method papers (not one) address the complete-case selection problem under explicit missingness models. Tompsett et al. (2023) formalize bias from missing eligibility in a point-treatment TTE, show patterns under MAR and MNAR, and evaluate multiple imputation of the eligibility-defining variables plus MNAR sensitivity shifts; they state that MNAR imputation remains exploratory because the sensitivity parameters are not identified from the data alone. Benz et al. (2025; also arXiv:2406.16830), which the entry cites as the first direct treatment, develops inverse-probability-of-ascertainment weights for sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption (ascertainment independent of true eligibility given non-eligibility covariates and treatment), evaluates them in plasmode EHR simulations, and applies them to a Kaiser Permanente bariatric-surgery cohort; accompanying research code is on GitHub (lbenz730/missing_eligibility_tte), not a production CRAN/Python package. Shen et al. (2026, Stat Med) compares complete-case analysis with three multiple-imputation strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs and reports that flexible MI often reduces bias when missingness is high. Wang et al. (2026) map eligibility realization in EHR data and cite Tompsett and Benz as the handling literature; they do not add a new estimator. What remains open, and matches the entry’s harder claim, is latent eligibility: an absent lab is consistent with never-tested versus would-have-failed, with recording driven by the same severity that predicts treatment and outcome (MNAR not cured by MAR IPW or standard MI). No paper retrieved jointly models true eligibility and its observation process anchored to a validation source where the criterion was assessed for everyone; no head-to-head of MI, IPW, doubly robust selection correction, and partial-identification bounds on the same TTE data with reporting of the implied eligible population under each method was found. Package search (TrialEmulation, WeightIt missing-covariate handling, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, zEpid, causallib) shows no shipped inverse-probability-of-eligibility-ascertainment or joint latent-eligibility measurement model. 2025–2026 guidance (TARGET, FDA RWE/ECT, EMA registry, NICE RWE) does not resolve identification of latent eligibility. Partial solve covers MAR complete-case selection; the title problem (unrecorded criterion indistinguishable from met criterion) stays open. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwac202: Partial: identifies and simulates selection bias from missing eligibility in TTE; evaluates MI of eligibility-defining variables and MNAR sensitivity imputation for recovering the eligible-population ACE under stated MAR/MNAR mechanisms (point treatment, continuous/binary outcome setting).. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwae471: Partial: IPW framework for selection due to incomplete eligibility ascertainment in sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption; simulation evaluation and real EHR application. Does not identify effects when missingness depends on latent eligibility itself.. Cites 10.1002/sim.70500: Partial: compares complete-case analysis versus three MI strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs; empirical guidance on when flexible MI reduces bias under high missingness. Still imputes recorded values rather than separating latent eligibility from observation.. Cites arxiv:2406.16830: Same as Benz 2025 AJE; states the eligibility-MAR assumption used by the weights and makes clear that standard complete-case analysis targets a different estimand (eligible complete cases, not all eligible)..

GLM-5.2, third independent lens

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and pitched at the right level of generality. It correctly identifies that restricting to complete cases selects on healthcare utilization, and that the latent eligibility problem is distinct from simple missingness. The stated reasons for the problem being open (MAR is not credible, validation sources are rare, and imputing a value is different from imputing eligibility) logically entail that the problem remains open. The claim does not assert an impossibility but rather a current methodological gap and a structural difficulty in distinguishing latent states from missing measurements.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text: DTA-02 Partially addressed High priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Statement
Distributed health data improve power and support transportability, and patient-level sharing is often prohibited, which is why federated emulation has been proposed and demonstrated for distributed effect estimation. The statistical machinery for combining site estimates is not the hard part. The hard part is that sites differ in coding systems, treatment availability, confounding structure and time resolution, so the same executable protocol can define materially different eligibility, exposure and outcome at each site. Averaging the resulting estimates produces a number whose estimand is the average of several different questions, and nothing in the aggregation step detects that.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Why it is open
The incompatibility is semantic rather than statistical: two sites can both return well-estimated, internally valid effects for populations the protocol was not intended to distinguish, and no summary of the estimates reveals it. The diagnostics that would reveal it require the patient-level data that federation exists to keep local. Heterogeneity statistics cannot separate real effect modification from mapping failure, since both produce between-site variance.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Li, et al. Federated target trial emulation using distributed observational data for treatment effect estimation. npj Digit Med 2025
Demonstrates that distributed effect estimation for an emulated trial is feasible without pooling patient-level data.


Manke-Reimers M, et al. When, why and how are estimated effects transported between populations? A scoping review. Eur J Epidemiol 2025
Reviews transport practice, which is the framework needed to say what a multi-site average is an estimate of.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Combine federated nuisance estimation with site-specific diagnostics and an explicit transport model, so the pooled quantity is a transported effect for a stated target population rather than an unweighted average. Share sufficient statistics, influence curves and aggregate balance measures, which is enough to diagnose incompatibility without moving patient records. Gate secure aggregation behind site-level trial-component validation: a site that fails the fitness check contributes to the report and not to the estimate.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Federated emulation has advanced past the feasibility demonstration the entry cites. POLARIS supplies a one-shot likelihood approach for federated emulation with time-to-event outcomes that claims pooled-equivalent estimates, and a 2026 JAMIA paper sets out ten principles for high-quality multi-site studies using privacy-preserving distributed algorithms, which is directly the site-validation discipline the entry asks for. The entry’s specific claim, that averaging site estimates can conceal that sites emulated different trials and that nothing in the aggregation detects it, is not answered by either: both improve the statistics of pooling rather than detecting semantic incompatibility. Cites 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9613167/v1: Provides pooled-equivalent federated estimation for emulated trials with survival outcomes, well past feasibility.. Cites 10.1093/jamia/ocag119: Codifies multi-site conduct including site-level validation, which is the gate the entry proposes..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The central warning is correct: operational differences can make site-specific estimates contrasts for different populations, interventions, outcomes, or follow-up regimes. A pooled result is still mathematically an average under specified weights, but it is not automatically an effect for a scientifically meaningful target population. Heterogeneity statistics cannot identify whether variation reflects effect modification, sampling error, positivity problems, or semantic mapping failure. The impossibility claim is too strong, however. Patient-level centralization is not required for all relevant diagnostics; sites can return cohort attrition, prevalence, support, balance, event rates, code-set provenance, and other privacy-preserving summaries after local validation. Conversely, sufficient statistics, influence curves, and balance summaries are not enough to establish semantic equivalence. A transport model also cannot repair incorrectly defined variables and requires explicit target-population and effect-modification assumptions. The open problem is reliable semantic validation and governance under federation, not the complete absence of diagnostics.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. The report’s own cited work, Li et al. (FL-TTE, 2025), demonstrates that distributed effect estimation for an emulated trial is feasible without pooling patient-level data. That is estimation machinery, not a solution to semantic incompatibility: sites can still implement different eligibility, exposure, or outcome mappings under the same executable protocol, and averaging site estimates does not detect that. Manke-Reimers et al. (2025) is a scoping review of transportability practice; it clarifies when a multi-site average needs an explicit transport model, but does not supply site-level diagnostics that separate mapping failure from true effect modification using only the aggregates federation is allowed to share. Recent federated causal-inference methods (for example Khellaf, Bellet, and Josse on propensity-score aggregation across sites; LATTE one-shot federated TTE showcased at OHDSI 2025) again address statistical pooling and privacy-preserving nuisance estimation, not semantic trial equivalence. Queries across AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/EJE/PDS/SiM, arXiv stat.ME, medRxiv, and package ecosystems (TrialEmulation, lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, gfoRmula) did not surface a released method that gates secure aggregation behind site-level trial-component validation or that diagnoses coding-system and phenotype discordance from sufficient statistics and aggregate balance alone. Heterogeneity statistics remain confounded between real effect modification and mapping failure, exactly as the problem states. Status remains open as stated.

GLM-5.2, third independent lens

open / supported. The claim is coherent and pitched at the right level of generality. It accurately identifies that the core difficulty in federated emulation is semantic incompatibility rather than statistical combination. The reasons given for it being open (diagnostics require patient-level data that federation restricts, and heterogeneity statistics conflate mapping failure with effect modification) directly support the claim that the problem remains open.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1/4) → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text: CNF-01 Overstated High priority Established Tractability 4/5

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Statement
The observational analogue of an intention-to-treat effect contrasts assigning initiation now against not initiating now. Two things then happen that do not happen in a randomized trial. Assignment is confounded, so the contrast requires baseline adjustment to mean anything. And the comparator group does not stay untreated: patients assigned to no initiation now frequently initiate later, so with longer follow-up the two strategies converge and the estimated effect attenuates toward the null for reasons that have nothing to do with the treatment’s efficacy. The attenuation is a function of the follow-up horizon and of local prescribing behavior, and it is rarely reported as such, so an emulation with long follow-up and a null result cannot be distinguished from one where the treatment does not work.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Why it is open
The convergence is a real feature of the strategy contrast rather than a bias to be removed, so it cannot be adjusted away without changing to a per-protocol estimand that carries its own assumptions. Reporting it requires publishing the treatment trajectories in both arms over follow-up, which most papers do not, and the rate of convergence depends on the health system and calendar period rather than on anything intrinsic. There is also no convention for choosing the horizon at which the contrast is still meaningful.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Hernán MA, Robins JM. Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 2016;183(8):758-764
Defines the observational analogues of the intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects and states what each requires.


Cain LE, Robins JM, Lanoy E, Logan R, Costagliola D, Hernán MA. Using observational data to emulate a randomized trial of dynamic treatment-switching strategies. Int J Epidemiol 2016;45(6):2038-2049
Handles later initiation and switching explicitly through dynamic strategies, which is the design response to convergence.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Report the cumulative incidence of initiation in both arms over follow-up alongside the effect estimate, so a reader can see how far the strategies remained distinct. Prefer strategy contrasts that name the later initiation explicitly, such as initiate now versus initiate on a stated clinical trigger, over an open-ended no-initiation arm that the data will not sustain. Quantify by simulation how much attenuation a given convergence rate produces at each horizon, so that a null result can be read against the convergence that was observed rather than against an assumption of none.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Our study

A single cumulative-initiation number at the horizon does not determine the attenuation it is asked to explain
The question put to it. CNF-01 asks authors to publish the cumulative incidence of initiation in both arms so a reader can see how far the contrasted strategies stayed distinct, and to quantify by simulation how much attenuation a given convergence rate produces. Does that diagnostic actually recover the attenuation?
What it found. No. Within the simulated grid, comparator-arm cumulative initiation at 120 months does not uniquely determine attenuation: matched early and late initiation scenarios, whose reported diagnostic agrees to within 0.0005, differ in attenuation by 0.0528 to 0.2027. Nine of the twelve matched pairs exceed the 0.05 threshold declared before the run by at least three Monte Carlo standard errors, at 5 to 46 of them; the other three sit within 3 and are individually inconclusive, and all three are at the lowest convergence rate, where there is least attenuation to misattribute. A single cumulative-incidence value at the horizon is therefore insufficient for recovering attenuation in these scenarios. What the reported number cannot see is when the comparator arm initiated and who initiated.
Results.

The insufficiency scales with convergence, which is the opposite of reassuring. At 20 percent cumulative initiation the matched difference is 0.053 to 0.070 and only one of four pairs is established; at 45 percent it is 0.116 to 0.145 at 18 to 27 Monte Carlo standard errors; at 70 percent it is 0.181 to 0.203 at 39 to 46. The diagnostic is least informative exactly where attenuation is largest.
Attenuation is large and grows with the horizon. Pooled across scenarios its median is 0.024 at one year and 0.245 at ten, with a maximum of 0.567. A treatment that genuinely works can lose more than half its sustained-strategy effect to convergence alone.
Who initiates matters as much as when. Concentrating initiation in high-risk patients raises attenuation from 0.476 to 0.567 at the highest convergence rate. The reported diagnostic, measured among observed non-initiators, stays at 0.700, while initiation under assignment to not initiating reaches 0.742: baseline confounding leaves lower-risk patients in the observed comparator arm, so the reported number understates the convergence of the assigned strategy.
Effect persistence is the factor that matters least. Transient and legacy regimes differ in attenuation by at most 0.034, at 24 months while the 12-month ramp is still under way, and by at most 0.014 at 120 months, against a spread across scenarios of 0.16 at one year and 0.50 at ten.
The estimators show small finite-sample bias rather than none. Coverage runs 0.934 to 0.970 against a nominal 0.95 and convergence is complete, but 14 of 288 cells carry bias beyond three Monte Carlo standard errors, to a maximum of 4.2. That does not touch the decisive comparison, which uses attenuation enumerated from the mechanism at two million individuals per scenario rather than estimated attenuation.

Design.

Estimand

Risk difference at horizons of 1 to 10 years for assignment to initiate at baseline versus not, with later initiation left to run, against the always-treated versus never-treated contrast the comparator arm would have supported had it stayed untreated

Methods compared

g-formula standardization, stabilized IPTW

Data-generating mechanism

Discrete monthly time to 10 years, 4000 individuals per replicate, confounded baseline initiation, later initiation in the comparator arm, and a treatment that works. 24 scenarios crossing three convergence rates, two timing shapes tuned to the same cumulative initiation at the horizon, initiation that does or does not concentrate in high-risk patients, and two effect-persistence regimes. 1000 replicates each, 24,000 replicates in all. Truth enumerated from the mechanism at two million individuals per scenario rather than estimated from the replicates.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 24,000 replicates, 288,000 estimate rows


What this does not answer. The comparison holds the diagnostic fixed only at 120 months. At earlier horizons the early and late scenarios differ in observed cumulative initiation by as much as 0.269, so those contrasts are not comparisons at equal C(h) and cannot independently establish insufficiency there. The study establishes that C(120) alone is insufficient within this grid. It does not establish that reporting C is necessary, that the full initiation curve would be sufficient, or that a universal conversion from convergence to attenuation exists. The comparator arm converges upward and the treated arm never discontinues, so this is one direction of convergence only. There is no loss to follow-up and no competing event, both excluded so the attenuation is not confounded with a second mechanism. The scale is the risk difference throughout; a hazard ratio would mix this mechanism with non-collapsibility.
